screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model for CI and CD and then map that model to the AWS developer tools that implement it. Continuous Integration is the habit of frequently merging work into a shared repository and verifying each merge with automated builds and tests. Continuous Delivery extends that verification so every change is packaged and ready for release, and Continuous Deployment automates the final release step so passing changes reach users immediately. On AWS you combine CodeCommit for source, CodeBuild for building and testing, CodeDeploy for applying changes to compute, and CodePipeline to orchestrate the stages. Understanding these roles matters because it lets you design pipelines that catch defects early, reduce risky manual steps, and speed feature feedback. For example, a team that runs automated tests on every commit finds integration failures within minutes, not days, and that quick feedback avoids late-stage firefighting. As you proceed you'll see how to set up a basic CodeCommit repository, how the services connect, and what deployment strategies like in-place and blue/green mean in practice. Think about a recent bug that took days to reproduce — how might automation have shortened that cycle?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Introduction to CI/CD

Introduction to CI/CD on AWS

Build repeatable pipelines using CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline.

In this lesson

You will learn the roles of CI and CD, the AWS services that implement them, and a practical first activity to create a CodeCommit repository. The focus is on clear roles and reliable automation, not on a specific language or framework.

Why it matters

Automated pipelines reduce manual errors, speed time to users, and let teams focus on features rather than deployment mechanics.

Explore Key Topics
Source
CodeCommit: a secure Git host for your source.
Build
CodeBuild: compile, test, and produce artifacts.
Deploy
CodeDeploy & CodePipeline: orchestrate safe releases.
Visual Map
CodeCommit
CodeBuild → Artifacts
CodeDeploy + CodePipeline
Coming up

We will step through CI, then CD, examine each AWS tool, and finish with a hands-on CodeCommit activity you can repeat.

You'll also be able to describe why CI/CD shortens feedback loops, raises software quality, and reduces deployment risk using a concrete example of a team that runs automated tests on every commit. As you learn, reflect on how automation could change a recent release you worked on and what stage you would automate first.

screens.title: Continuous Integration (CI)
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration is a disciplined development practice where developers frequently merge their code changes into a central repository and each integration is verified by an automated build and test process. The core purpose is early detection: small, frequent merges make integration problems smaller and faster to fix. For example, imagine three engineers working on adjacent modules. If they integrate daily, automated builds will reveal a failing test within minutes of the breaking change, and the responsible developer can revert or fix that small change quickly. A common misconception is that CI only means automated builds; in reality, CI includes both build and automated tests, and sometimes static analysis or linting as part of the verification. Another pitfall is infrequent, large merges — those defeat CI's value because the integration surface is too large and debugging becomes slow. To get CI right, keep commits small, run a fast feedback test suite on every merge, and make build failures visible to the team. As a reflective question: what tests would you prioritize to get the fastest, most useful feedback on every merge?

keyIdea.title: CI in brief
keyIdea.text: Merge frequently, run automated builds and tests on each merge, and fix failures quickly to avoid late integration problems.

content.html:
Core Concept › Continuous Integration
What CI means

Frequent merges into a shared repo with automated build and test verification on each change.

  • • Small commits reduce integration surface and speed debugging.
  • • Automated tests run on every merge to catch regressions early.
  • • Build visibility ensures the team notices and fixes failures quickly.
Concrete example

Three engineers commit daily. A failing unit test immediately points to the recent change, so the fix takes minutes instead of days.

Common mistake

Treating CI as only a build step without meaningful automated tests defeats the purpose of early feedback.

Pipeline snapshot
Source: CodeCommit

Developers push changes that trigger the CI run.

Checks performed
  • • Build artifacts created to validate compilation.
  • • Automated unit and integration tests run to catch regressions.
  • • Test failures block the change until resolved.
Key Takeaway

CI gives you fast, repeatable feedback on integration problems so teams can fix issues quickly and safely.

screens.title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment share a common pipeline up to test and packaging. The difference is the final gate. Continuous Delivery ensures every change is automatically built, tested, and packaged so the team can release to production at any time, but the actual production deployment remains a manual decision. Continuous Deployment removes that manual gate and automatically deploys every change that passes the automated checks. A concrete scenario: a team with mature automated tests and robust monitoring may adopt Continuous Deployment to shorten feedback loops, delivering small changes to customers multiple times per day. A team handling sensitive data or complex migrations might prefer Continuous Delivery with a manual approval step to coordinate database changes and stakeholder notification. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment is always faster without trade-offs; in fact, it demands stronger test coverage, observability, and rollback plans. The practical takeaway is to choose the level of automation that matches your team's test maturity and operational readiness, and then iterate by adding safety nets like feature flags or gradual traffic shifts. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment means delivery = always releasable; deployment = automatically released. choose based on test maturity and rollback ability.. In practical terms, a practical contrast and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Difference
keyIdea.text: Delivery = always releasable; Deployment = automatically released. Choose based on test maturity and rollback ability.

content.html:
Comparison › Delivery vs Deployment
Continuous Delivery

Automated build, test, and packaging so every change is releasable; deployment to production is a manual step.

• Use when you need human oversight for production changes.
• Benefits: predictable releases and safer coordination for risky changes.
• Example: major schema migration requiring scheduled downtime.
Continuous Deployment

Automates the final deployment so any change that passes automated checks goes to production immediately.

• Use when tests, monitoring, and rollback are strong and you want rapid feedback from users.
• Benefits: faster time to market and smaller, easier-to-debug changes.
• Example: well-covered microservice that can be rolled back quickly if issues appear.
Misconception check

Continuous Deployment is not simply faster; it requires investment in test coverage, monitoring, and rollback strategies. If those are missing, automated deployment increases risk.

Key Takeaway

Match the pipeline's final gate to your team's ability to detect and respond to problems rapidly.

screens.title: AWS CodeCommit — Source Control
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeCommit is a fully managed source control service that hosts secure, private Git repositories. Within CI/CD, the repository is the canonical source: it stores your code, configuration, and often infrastructure as code artifacts that trigger the pipeline. The practical benefit of using a managed service is you avoid operating your own Git servers while still supporting standard Git workflows. For example, when a developer pushes an initial commit to a CodeCommit repository, that push becomes the event that triggers CodePipeline to start a build. A misconception is that a managed Git service removes the need for repository hygiene; you still need small commits, clear commit messages, and sensible branching strategies. Also keep credentials and IAM permissions scoped so the pipeline only has the access it needs. In short, treat CodeCommit as the authoritative source for your pipeline and maintain good Git practices so the automation gives you reliable, auditable releases. AWS CodeCommit — Source Control means managed git repository that acts as the source of truth and triggers pipeline runs when changes are pushed.. In practical terms, a managed git service for your pipeline's source stage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Managed Git repository that acts as the source of truth and triggers pipeline runs when changes are pushed.

content.html:
Definition › AWS CodeCommit
What CodeCommit provides

Private Git repositories that integrate with your CI/CD pipeline and trigger downstream automation on changes.

• Acts as the canonical source for code and configuration.
• Triggers pipeline execution when commits or branches change.
• Works with standard Git workflows so teams need not change tools.
Best practice

Use small commits, clear messages, and branch policies to ensure automation runs on high-quality changes.

Concrete flow
  1. A developer commits and pushes code to CodeCommit.
  2. The push triggers CodePipeline or a Cloud event to start build and test stages.
  3. Artifacts are produced for deployment if checks pass.
Common mistake

Relying on a single long-lived branch for all development removes the benefits of frequent integration and reduces visibility into individual changes.

Key Takeaway

Use CodeCommit as the trusted source and practice Git hygiene to make automation reliable.

screens.title: AWS CodeBuild — Building and Testing
screens.narratorSegment: CodeBuild is a managed continuous integration service that compiles source, runs tests, and produces artifacts ready for deployment. It removes the need to administer build servers by running build environments on demand and scaling automatically. The important conceptual point is that CodeBuild turns committed source into validated deliverables: it runs your test suite, fails the build if tests fail, and emits artifacts that downstream stages consume. A concrete example is a build that runs unit and integration tests and then packages compiled binaries or zipped application bundles for deployment. A common misconception is that builds must be slow or heavyweight; in practice you should design fast, meaningful test suites for CI so feedback arrives quickly. Another pitfall is coupling environment-specific setup into the build; prefer reproducible build definitions so every build environment behaves the same. The practical outcome is predictable artifacts and quicker bug detection, which together shorten release cycles and reduce deployment surprises. AWS CodeBuild — Building and Testing means execute builds and tests in managed environments and produce deterministic artifacts that downstream stages deploy.. In practical terms, how managed builds produce artifacts for deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CodeBuild role
keyIdea.text: Execute builds and tests in managed environments and produce deterministic artifacts that downstream stages deploy.

content.html:
Process Flow › CodeBuild
What CodeBuild does

Runs builds and tests in managed, scalable environments and outputs deployable artifacts.

• Runs your defined build steps and test commands.
• Fails early on test regressions so changes don't progress to deploy.
• Produces artifacts consumed by CodeDeploy or other deploy stages.
Design tip

Keep CI tests fast and focused. Use nightly pipelines for long-running integration tests to avoid blocking rapid feedback.

Example build flow
# build steps (illustrative)
install dependencies
run unit tests
run static analysis
package artifacts

This block shows a typical sequence of build actions; your project will replace these with concrete commands.

Common pitfall

Long-running tests in the CI loop delay feedback. Use fast checks in CI and schedule heavier tests separately.

Key Takeaway

Use CodeBuild to produce repeatable, tested artifacts so downstream deployments are predictable.

screens.title: AWS CodeDeploy — Deployment Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: CodeDeploy automates application deployments to compute targets like virtual machines, containers, or functions. Two deployment strategies are commonly used: in-place and blue/green. In-place deployment updates the existing instances in place, replacing application files and restarting services. It is simple but can cause brief downtime if the update is not orchestrated carefully. Blue/green deployment directs traffic to a fresh environment while keeping the old environment available to roll back quickly if problems appear. Blue/green minimizes user impact and supports quick rollbacks at the cost of extra infrastructure during the switch. A practical example: for a stateless microservice, blue/green allows a quick shift of traffic to the new version and instant rollback if monitoring detects errors. A common misconception is that blue/green always eliminates risk; it reduces user-facing risk but requires planning for data migrations and stateful components. Choose the strategy that balances your tolerance for downtime, infrastructure cost, and rollback complexity. AWS CodeDeploy — Deployment Strategies means in-place updates are simpler; blue/green reduces downtime and enables fast rollback but may require duplicate infrastructure.. In practical terms, in-place and blue/green strategies and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment choices
keyIdea.text: In-place updates are simpler; blue/green reduces downtime and enables fast rollback but may require duplicate infrastructure.

content.html:
Definition › CodeDeploy Strategies
In-place deployment

Updates existing instances directly; simpler but can cause short downtime unless carefully managed.

• Lower infrastructure cost since no duplicate environment is required.
• Rollback may be more complex if artifacts overwrite in place.
• Best for small, well-tested updates where brief restarts are acceptable.
Blue/green deployment

Deploy to a separate environment and switch traffic when the new version is ready, enabling quick rollback if needed.

• Minimizes user impact during release and supports instant rollback.
• Requires duplicate resources and traffic management.
• Preferred for high-availability services with strict uptime requirements.
Practical note

Consider data migration and stateful components when choosing a strategy. Blue/green helps with stateless services, while in-place may suffice for simple updates.

Key Takeaway

Match deployment strategy to service characteristics: use blue/green for minimal downtime, in-place for cost simplicity.

screens.title: AWS CodePipeline — Orchestrating the Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: CodePipeline is the orchestration service that defines and automates the flow of changes through the release stages. It connects source, build, test, and deploy steps into a repeatable sequence so that every change follows the same path from commit to production. Conceptually, think of CodePipeline as the conductor that wires CodeCommit events to CodeBuild jobs, collects artifacts, and invokes deployments through CodeDeploy. A concrete example: a push to a CodeCommit repository triggers CodePipeline, which invokes CodeBuild to run tests and package artifacts; if tests pass, CodePipeline advances the artifact to a deploy stage that uses CodeDeploy. A common misunderstanding is that orchestration removes the need to design each stage carefully; in fact, orchestration exposes weaknesses if stages lack adequate tests or observability. To design reliable pipelines, define clear artifacts, fail fast when tests fail, and use stage gates for manual approvals when needed. The practical result is predictable, repeatable releases that can be audited and improved incrementally. AWS CodePipeline — Orchestrating the Pipeline means codepipeline wires source, build, test, and deploy stages so changes flow automatically and consistently through the release process.. In practical terms, how stages connect to automate releases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture › CodePipeline
Pipeline stages
Source
Build
Test
Deploy
• CodePipeline enforces a consistent path for every change so releases are repeatable.
• Artifacts produced by the build stage are the single source for deployment stages.
• Manual approval gates can be added to control production releases.
Concrete example

A commit triggers CodePipeline, CodeBuild runs tests and packages artifacts, and CodeDeploy updates instances if checks pass.

Pro tip

Make artifacts immutable and versioned so every stage operates on the same, auditable inputs.

Key Takeaway

Use CodePipeline to enforce repeatable delivery paths and to integrate tools into a single automated workflow.

screens.title: Typical CI/CD Pipeline Stages
screens.narratorSegment: A typical CI/CD pipeline follows a clear sequence: source, build, test, and deploy. The source stage captures changes in your Version Control System and starts the pipeline. The build stage compiles code and prepares artifacts. The test stage runs automated checks—unit tests and lightweight integration tests should run in CI—while heavier system tests may run separately. Finally, the deploy stage applies validated artifacts to target environments using a chosen strategy. A concrete example: a developer pushes a change to CodeCommit (source), CodeBuild compiles and runs unit tests (build/test), artifacts pass to CodePipeline which triggers CodeDeploy to update staging or production (deploy). A common mistake is mixing long-running tests into the CI loop; this delays feedback. Instead, keep the CI loop fast with core checks and run longer tests on a scheduled pipeline. Another practical detail is ensuring artifacts are versioned and immutable so rollbacks and audits are straightforward. The takeaway is to design each stage for speed, determinism, and clear responsibilities. screens.title: Designing Reliable Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: Reliable pipelines are intentionally designed for fast feedback, clear ownership, and safe deployments. Start by keeping the CI loop fast: prioritize unit tests and quick integration checks so failures are visible within minutes. Separate longer-running system tests into nightly or scheduled pipelines to avoid blocking development. Version and immutably store artifacts so what you test is exactly what you deploy. Add observability to each stage: make build logs, test results, and deployment outputs easy to find and correlate. Use stage gates and manual approvals when production changes require coordination, and employ deployment strategies like blue/green when you need minimal downtime. A typical misconception is that automation alone guarantees safety; automation must be paired with monitoring, rollback plans, and predictable artifacts. Finally, practice small, frequent releases and rely on feature flags for risky changes. The ultimate measure is the velocity of safe releases: if automation increases your ability to ship and roll back quickly, it's working correctly. Best Practices › Designing Reliable Pipelines
Core practices

  • • Immutable artifacts: build once and promote the same artifact through stages.
  • • Observability: surface logs and test outputs for quick diagnosis.
  • • Deployment safety: use blue/green or approvals where rollback or downtime risk is high.
  • • Small releases and feature flags: reduce blast radius and enable safe experimentation.
Common mistake

Automating fragile stages without improving tests and monitoring creates brittle pipelines that fail silently or cause harm.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Pipeline failures happen, and diagnosing them quickly keeps releases on schedule. Start by reading the failure's context: build logs show compilation and test output; test failures often include stack traces or failing assertions that reveal the cause. If a deployment fails, check deployment logs and health checks for the target environment. A frequent human mistake is treating pipeline failures as infrastructure problems before confirming whether a code change introduced the issue. Another common error is inadequate test coverage that lets regressions slip into deploy stages. To improve resilience, add clear logging to builds and tests, version artifacts so you can redeploy a known-good version, and create small rollbackable releases. Use a stepwise approach: reproduce the failure locally against the same artifact, inspect logs, and then fix either the code or the pipeline configuration. The final question for you: when a pipeline fails in your project, what is the first piece of information you would inspect and why? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model for CI and CD and then map that model to the AWS developer tools that implement it. Continuous Integration is the habit of frequently merging work into a shared repository and verifying each merge with automated builds and tests. Continuous Delivery extends that verification so every change is packaged and ready for release, and Continuous Deployment automates the final release step so passing changes reach users immediately. On AWS you combine CodeCommit for source, CodeBuild for building and testing, CodeDeploy for applying changes to compute, and CodePipeline to orchestrate the stages. Understanding these roles matters because it lets you design pipelines that catch defects early, reduce risky manual steps, and speed feature feedback. For example, a team that runs automated tests on every commit finds integration failures within minutes, not days, and that quick feedback avoids late-stage firefighting. As you proceed you'll see how to set up a basic CodeCommit repository, how the services connect, and what deployment strategies like in-place and blue/green mean in practice. Think about a recent bug that took days to reproduce — how might automation have shortened that cycle?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and explain the three core practices: Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment. You will identify the primary AWS developer tools—CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline—and explain what each service does within a release pipeline. You'll also be able to describe why CI/CD shortens feedback loops, raises software quality, and reduces deployment risk using a concrete example of a team that runs automated tests on every commit. Lastly, you will walk through the practical steps to create a simple CodeCommit repository and push an initial artifact so you can begin wiring a pipeline. These objectives matter because they turn abstract DevOps principles into repeatable steps you can apply to your projects. For instance, knowing when to use Continuous Delivery rather than Continuous Deployment helps you balance speed with safety. As you learn, reflect on how automation could change a recent release you worked on and what stage you would automate first.

This second objectives slide focuses on application and judgment. You'll learn to choose when to use Continuous Delivery versus Continuous Deployment based on team readiness and risk tolerance. You will also practice mapping service responsibilities so you can design a pipeline: CodeCommit hosts source, CodeBuild runs builds and tests, CodeDeploy applies updates to compute, and CodePipeline orchestrates those stages. You'll learn to read basic pipeline logs and artifacts so debugging becomes methodical rather than ad hoc. Finally, you'll reflect on one deployment strategy—blue/green versus in-place—and know the trade-offs in complexity and downtime. A practical example: if your team cannot instantly roll back a complex database change, Continuous Delivery with a manual production gate is often safer than full Continuous Deployment. These choices affect release frequency, operational effort, and customer risk. The goal is not blind automation but predictable, testable releases that support fast learning.

Continuous Integration is a disciplined development practice where developers frequently merge their code changes into a central repository and each integration is verified by an automated build and test process. The core purpose is early detection: small, frequent merges make integration problems smaller and faster to fix. For example, imagine three engineers working on adjacent modules. If they integrate daily, automated builds will reveal a failing test within minutes of the breaking change, and the responsible developer can revert or fix that small change quickly. A common misconception is that CI only means automated builds; in reality, CI includes both build and automated tests, and sometimes static analysis or linting as part of the verification. Another pitfall is infrequent, large merges — those defeat CI's value because the integration surface is too large and debugging becomes slow. To get CI right, keep commits small, run a fast feedback test suite on every merge, and make build failures visible to the team. As a reflective question: what tests would you prioritize to get the fastest, most useful feedback on every merge?

Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment share a common pipeline up to test and packaging. The difference is the final gate. Continuous Delivery ensures every change is automatically built, tested, and packaged so the team can release to production at any time, but the actual production deployment remains a manual decision. Continuous Deployment removes that manual gate and automatically deploys every change that passes the automated checks. A concrete scenario: a team with mature automated tests and robust monitoring may adopt Continuous Deployment to shorten feedback loops, delivering small changes to customers multiple times per day. A team handling sensitive data or complex migrations might prefer Continuous Delivery with a manual approval step to coordinate database changes and stakeholder notification. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment is always faster without trade-offs; in fact, it demands stronger test coverage, observability, and rollback plans. The practical takeaway is to choose the level of automation that matches your team's test maturity and operational readiness, and then iterate by adding safety nets like feature flags or gradual traffic shifts. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment means delivery = always releasable; deployment = automatically released. choose based on test maturity and rollback ability.. In practical terms, a practical contrast and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS CodeCommit is a fully managed source control service that hosts secure, private Git repositories. Within CI/CD, the repository is the canonical source: it stores your code, configuration, and often infrastructure as code artifacts that trigger the pipeline. The practical benefit of using a managed service is you avoid operating your own Git servers while still supporting standard Git workflows. For example, when a developer pushes an initial commit to a CodeCommit repository, that push becomes the event that triggers CodePipeline to start a build. A misconception is that a managed Git service removes the need for repository hygiene; you still need small commits, clear commit messages, and sensible branching strategies. Also keep credentials and IAM permissions scoped so the pipeline only has the access it needs. In short, treat CodeCommit as the authoritative source for your pipeline and maintain good Git practices so the automation gives you reliable, auditable releases. AWS CodeCommit — Source Control means managed git repository that acts as the source of truth and triggers pipeline runs when changes are pushed.. In practical terms, a managed git service for your pipeline's source stage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CodeBuild is a managed continuous integration service that compiles source, runs tests, and produces artifacts ready for deployment. It removes the need to administer build servers by running build environments on demand and scaling automatically. The important conceptual point is that CodeBuild turns committed source into validated deliverables: it runs your test suite, fails the build if tests fail, and emits artifacts that downstream stages consume. A concrete example is a build that runs unit and integration tests and then packages compiled binaries or zipped application bundles for deployment. A common misconception is that builds must be slow or heavyweight; in practice you should design fast, meaningful test suites for CI so feedback arrives quickly. Another pitfall is coupling environment-specific setup into the build; prefer reproducible build definitions so every build environment behaves the same. The practical outcome is predictable artifacts and quicker bug detection, which together shorten release cycles and reduce deployment surprises. AWS CodeBuild — Building and Testing means execute builds and tests in managed environments and produce deterministic artifacts that downstream stages deploy.. In practical terms, how managed builds produce artifacts for deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CodeDeploy automates application deployments to compute targets like virtual machines, containers, or functions. Two deployment strategies are commonly used: in-place and blue/green. In-place deployment updates the existing instances in place, replacing application files and restarting services. It is simple but can cause brief downtime if the update is not orchestrated carefully. Blue/green deployment directs traffic to a fresh environment while keeping the old environment available to roll back quickly if problems appear. Blue/green minimizes user impact and supports quick rollbacks at the cost of extra infrastructure during the switch. A practical example: for a stateless microservice, blue/green allows a quick shift of traffic to the new version and instant rollback if monitoring detects errors. A common misconception is that blue/green always eliminates risk; it reduces user-facing risk but requires planning for data migrations and stateful components. Choose the strategy that balances your tolerance for downtime, infrastructure cost, and rollback complexity. CodePipeline is the orchestration service that defines and automates the flow of changes through the release stages. It connects source, build, test, and deploy steps into a repeatable sequence so that every change follows the same path from commit to production. Conceptually, think of CodePipeline as the conductor that wires CodeCommit events to CodeBuild jobs, collects artifacts, and invokes deployments through CodeDeploy. A concrete example: a push to a CodeCommit repository triggers CodePipeline, which invokes CodeBuild to run tests and package artifacts; if tests pass, CodePipeline advances the artifact to a deploy stage that uses CodeDeploy. A common misunderstanding is that orchestration removes the need to design each stage carefully; in fact, orchestration exposes weaknesses if stages lack adequate tests or observability. To design reliable pipelines, define clear artifacts, fail fast when tests fail, and use stage gates for manual approvals when needed. The practical result is predictable, repeatable releases that can be audited and improved incrementally.
